related_questions.question: How does COVID affect diabetes?
related_questions.snippet: A: People with diabetes are more likely to have serious complications from COVID-19. In general, people with diabetes are more likely to have more severe symptoms and complications when infected with any virus. Your risk of getting very sick from COVID-19 is likely to be lower if your diabetes is well-managed.

related_questions.question: What should a diabetic do if they get COVID?
related_questions.snippet: Check your blood sugar more often than usual. COVID-19 can reduce your appetite and cause you to eat less, which could affect your levels. You also need more fluids than usual when you're sick. Keep water close by, and drink it often.

related_questions.question: What virus triggers diabetes?
related_questions.snippet: Several viruses have been associated with Type 1 diabetes, but one type of virus, called Human Enteroviruses (HEVs), have the strongest body of evidence. HEVs are a large family of viruses that enter the gut and are spread through poor hygiene or sanitation.

related_questions.question: What happens when a diabetic gets sick?

text_blocks.snippet: When someone with diabetes gets sick, their blood sugar levels can become difficult to manage due to the body's stress response to illness. This can lead to either high or low blood sugar, and in some cases, diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), a serious complication. It's crucial for individuals with diabetes to have a sick-day plan and closely monitor their blood glucose levels during illness.
snippet_highlighted_words: their blood sugar levels can become difficult to manage due to the body's stress response to illness

text_blocks.snippet: Here's a more detailed look at what can happen:

list.title: Increased Blood Sugar:
list.snippet: Illness triggers the release of stress hormones, which can increase blood sugar levels, even if the person isn't eating much.

list.title: Decreased Blood Sugar:
list.snippet: Vomiting, diarrhea, or not eating as usual can lead to low blood sugar (hypoglycemia).
DKA is a serious complication that can occur when the body doesn't have enough insulin to use glucose for energy, forcing it to break down fat for fuel instead.
This process produces ketones, which can make the blood acidic, leading to DKA.
Symptoms of DKA include excessive thirst, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, weakness, shortness of breath, and a fruity-smelling breath.
DKA is a medical emergency requiring immediate attention, according to the Cleveland Clinic.

list.title: Follow a Sick Day Plan:
list.snippet: Individuals with diabetes should have a pre-determined plan from their doctor for managing their diabetes during illness.

list.title: Monitor Blood Sugar Frequently:
list.snippet: Check blood sugar levels regularly, often more frequently than usual, to catch any fluctuations early.

list.title: Stay Hydrated:
list.snippet: Drink plenty of fluids, especially if experiencing vomiting or diarrhea.

list.title: Continue Insulin:
list.snippet: Do not stop taking insulin, even if you're not eating much, as your body still needs it to process glucose.

list.title: Check for Ketones:
list.snippet: Test urine for ketones, especially if blood sugar levels are high or if you're experiencing symptoms of DKA.

list.title: Seek Medical Advice:
list.snippet: Consult a doctor or diabetes care team if you experience persistent high or low blood sugar, vomiting, diarrhea, or signs of DKA.

list.title: Children and Adolescents:
list.snippet: Kids with diabetes may be more susceptible to blood sugar fluctuations during illness and require extra attention to prevent complications.

list.title: COVID-19 and Flu:
list.snippet: People with diabetes are at higher risk for severe illness from COVID-19 and the flu and should prioritize vaccination and seek early medical care if they become sick.

text_blocks.snippet: By understanding the potential impacts of illness on blood sugar levels and following a well-defined sick-day plan, individuals with diabetes can minimize risks and manage their condition effectively during periods of sickness.

text_blocks.snippet: Diabetes and COVID-19 have a complex and interconnected relationship.
Increased Risk for People with Diabetes:

list.snippet: People with diabetes have a higher risk of developing severe complications from COVID-19, including hospitalization, intensive care unit (ICU) admission, and death.
This is because diabetes weakens the immune system and increases inflammation, making individuals more susceptible to infections and their complications.

text_blocks.snippet: Impact of COVID-19 on Diabetes Management:

list.snippet: COVID-19 infection can lead to changes in blood sugar levels, making it difficult to manage diabetes effectively.
Stress, illness, and changes in diet and activity patterns can all impact blood glucose control.
In some cases, COVID-19 can trigger or worsen type 2 diabetes.
Studies have shown that people who recover from COVID-19 may have an increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes in the future.
This may be due to changes in metabolic function and inflammation caused by the virus.
People with diabetes should follow all recommended precautions to prevent COVID-19, including vaccination, mask-wearing, and social distancing.
It is crucial for people with diabetes to maintain good blood glucose control and work closely with their healthcare team to manage their condition effectively.
If diagnosed with COVID-19, people with diabetes should seek medical attention promptly and follow their healthcare provider's instructions carefully.

text_blocks.snippet: Diabetes and COVID-19 have a significant relationship, with people with diabetes having a higher risk of severe complications from the virus. It is essential for individuals with diabetes to take steps to prevent infection, manage their condition effectively, and seek medical attention promptly if they develop COVID-19.
